title: Things Fall Apart
significance: It first establishes the order of an Igbo village and Okonkwo's downfall by internal logic before arranging for missionaries and colonial administration to arrive, so that the cause of collapse is never reduced to a single outside arrival. Handing the final two paragraphs over to the style of an administrator's report shows, as a matter of form, to whom the authority of narration has passed.

title: No Longer at Ease
significance: Through Okonkwo's grandson, who returns from studying in Britain to become a civil servant in Lagos, it traces backward from a courtroom scene how the generation just before independence is undone by a single corruption case. It is the only volume of the trilogy to deal with the time of the city and the salaried worker.

title: Arrow of God
significance: It deals with how religious authority collapses by its own hand when colonial indirect rule tries to absorb a village's priesthood into an administrative unit. Of his novels, it narrates the internal politics of Igbo society and the language of oracles in the closest detail.

title: A Man of the People
significance: It treats the patronage politics and corruption of a post-independence politician through first-person satire and ends with a military coup; an actual coup took place in Nigeria immediately after publication, which changed the book's standing.

title: An Image of Africa: Racism in Conrad's Heart of Darkness
significance: First delivered as a 1975 lecture and set in print in 1977. Reading a landmark work of the Western canon as a text that uses Africa as mere scenery, it made rereading the canon a formal procedure of literary criticism.

title: Anthills of the Savannah
significance: It treats the military regime of a fictional country through a structure of four alternating character viewpoints, a late major work that shifts the focus his earlier novels placed on village and individual onto the workings of state power.

title: Midaq Alley
significance: Set entirely in one narrow Cairo alley during the Second World War, it arranges in parallel the failed attempts of its characters to escape that alley. An early major work in which Mahfouz's urban realism appears in complete form within a single book.

title: Palace Walk
significance: Part one of the Cairo Trilogy. Set against the 1919 revolution, it accumulates the day-to-day life of the patriarch Abd al-Jawad's family, narrating the way political history arrives by way of domestic discipline.

title: Palace of Desire
significance: Part two of the trilogy. Set in the 1920s, when the son's generation splits between secular learning and religion, it narrates through alternating character viewpoints the process by which the patriarch's authority is shaken from within.

title: Sugar Street
significance: Part three of the trilogy. Set in the 1930s and 40s, when the grandsons' generation splits between communism and the Muslim Brotherhood, it closes by overlaying three generations' time with the branching paths of modern Egyptian political history.

title: Children of the Alley
significance: A work that transposes the history of the monotheistic religions into allegory through the generational succession of a single alley. After its 1959 newspaper serialization it could not appear as a book in Egypt for a long time because of backlash from religious circles, and it circulated instead through a 1967 Beirut edition.

title: Notebook of a Return to the Native Land
significance: The long poem in which the word 'Négritude' first appears. It takes a structure that opens with the gaze of a return to Martinique, enumerates the colony's deprivations, and then turns into a declaration of Blackness; revisions in 1947 and 1956 changed its lines substantially.

title: Miraculous Weapons
significance: His first regular poetry collection, filling chains of imagery close to Surrealist automatic writing with the vocabulary of Caribbean volcanoes, plants, and sea. It shows most clearly that Césaire's poetry is at once political speech and avant-garde experiment.

title: Discourse on Colonialism
significance: A short essay that struck back at European humanism's self-image with the argument that colonial rule barbarizes the colonizer before it destroys the colonized. Its expanded 1955 edition was widely read.

title: The Tragedy of King Christophe
significance: Through Henri Christophe, who became king after the Haitian Revolution, it stages the process by which a nation founded by the freed produces forced labor and hierarchy all over again. It is the starting point of Césaire's trilogy of plays on power after decolonization.

title: A Tempest
significance: An adaptation of Shakespeare's The Tempest rewritten for a Black theater company. Casting Caliban as the rebelling colonized subject and Ariel as the compromising mixed-race intellectual, it turns the original's very cast of roles into a diagram of colonial relations.

title: The Lion and the Jewel
significance: A comedy in which a village chief and a Western-educated schoolteacher compete over one woman, overturning the scheme that casts modernization as a conflict between progress and tradition. It premiered in Ibadan in 1959 and was published in 1963.

title: A Dance of the Forests
significance: Written as a commission for Nigeria's independence celebrations, it turns the founding celebration into a warning by arranging for the summoned ancestors to testify to past violence rather than glory. The time structure distinctive to Soyinka, in which the living and the dead share one stage, is brought fully to the fore here for the first time.

title: The Man Died: Prison Notes
significance: A prose record of nearly two years of imprisonment without trial during the Biafran War. It takes the very conditions of writing notes in solitary confinement, through hunger strikes and past censorship, as its form of narration.

title: A Shuttle in the Crypt
significance: A collection of poems written during his imprisonment. Comparing the confined mind to the back-and-forth motion of a weaver's shuttle, it records the same events as the prose account in a language of an entirely different density.

title: Death and the King's Horseman
significance: It deals with the catastrophe that follows when a colonial administrator halts the ritual by which a king's horseman must die to follow him. Soyinka explicitly rejected readings of the play as a clash of cultures, placing the axis of the action in the Yoruba rite of passage itself.

title: Aké: The Years of Childhood
significance: A memoir that restores, from a child's point of view, a childhood spent in the mission compound at Abeokuta. By narrating a state in which the Yoruba spirit world and an English-style school coexist within a single child's day, it shows the grounding for the layered worlds his plays deal with.

title: Weep Not, Child
significance: A novel that narrates the Mau Mau uprising and the state of emergency from the viewpoint of a boy trying to attend school. It is recorded as the first novel published in English by an East African writer.

title: A Grain of Wheat
significance: Over four days leading up to Independence Day, it takes a structure in which four characters' pasts intersect and the identity of an informer is revealed. A turning point that places betrayal and silence, rather than a heroic narrative, at the center of the history of independence.

title: Petals of Blood
significance: A novel that uses a murder investigation as its frame to deal with land concentration and rising capital in Kenya after independence. It is the last novel he published in English.

title: I Will Marry When I Want
significance: A Gikuyu-language play co-written with Ngũgĩ wa Mĩriĩ and performed by the residents of Kamiriithu village themselves. The theater was demolished immediately after the performance and the author was imprisoned without trial, an event that triggered his switch of language. The Gikuyu script was published in 1980.

title: Devil on the Cross
significance: A Gikuyu-language novel written on toilet paper during his imprisonment at Kamiti Prison. Using the allegorical device of a thieves' competition and the repetition and exaggeration of oral performance as its novelistic structure, it demonstrated in the flesh that Gikuyu prose could carry a novel.

title: Decolonising the Mind: The Politics of Language in African Literature
significance: A collection of essays that starts from the experience of colonial education making the mother tongue an object of punishment, and argues that African literature remains cut off from its readers as long as it is written in a European language. In the preface he announced he would stop writing in English.

title: The Doum Tree of Wad Hamid
significance: A short story in which villagers refuse when the government tries to cut down the village tree and build a modern facility. It is the first appearance of the fictional village of Wad Hamid, which recurs across several later works.

title: The Wedding of Zein
significance: A novella that narrates, by joining together the testimony of several villagers, how Zein, once the village's laughingstock, comes to marry its most beautiful woman. An early instance of Salih carrying the manner of oral storytelling into the structure of fiction.

title: Season of Migration to the North
significance: A frame novel in which a nameless narrator back home belatedly reconstructs the past of a man returned from London. It reverses the route toward empire, moving the metaphor of conquest into the bedroom and the courtroom, and leaves its ending unresolved in the middle of a river rather than as a verdict. It was first published in a Beirut magazine.

title: Bandarshah
significance: The first volume of a two-part work dealing with generational conflict in the village of Wad Hamid; the second volume appeared in 1976. Scattering chronological order and mixing dream and genealogy, it moves in the direction of dismantling the village his earlier works had built.

title: Dream on Monkey Mountain
significance: Structured around a jailed charcoal seller who dreams of becoming an African king, it interrogates on stage the very demand for a recovery of Blackness. It is the major play Walcott made together with his Trinidad theater company.

title: Another Life
significance: A long autobiographical poem dealing with a childhood spent wanting to become a painter, a mentor, and the light of the island. His position that naming the Caribbean landscape is the poet's first task takes shape here.

title: The Star-Apple Kingdom
significance: In the collected poem 'The Schooner Flight,' the Creole voice of the sailor Shabine holds Caribbean race, history, and migration within a single poem. The method of alternating standard English and Creole within a single line appears here most clearly.

title: Omeros
significance: A long epic poem, narrated in terza rima, that gives the names of Achilles, Hector, and Helen to fishermen of St. Lucia. Placing Homer not as an object of quotation but on the same plane as the island's daily life, it redefines the form of the European epic as a matter of inheritance.

title: White Egrets
significance: A late poetry collection dealing with old age, the deaths of friends, and the light of the island. It shows the form of his final years, having stripped away his earlier narrative ambition to return to short stanzas of observation and mourning.
